title: de Natura Deorum
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi050.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: nec vero probare soleo id quod de Pythagoreis accepimus, quos ferunt, si quid adfirmarent in disputando, cum ex iis quaereretur quare ita esset, respondere solitos ipse dixit; ipse autem erat Pythagoras: tantum opinio praeiudicata poterat, ut etiam sine ratione valeret auctoritas.
passages.english: Nor indeed am I accustomed to approve what we have heard about the Pythagoreans, who, they say, if they asserted anything in debate and were asked why it was so, used to reply "He himself said [it]"; and "he himself" was Pythagoras: so much power did a prejudged opinion have that authority prevailed even without reason.

passages.original: Tum Velleius fidenter sane, ut solent isti, nihil tam verens quam ne dubitare aliqua de re videretur, tamquam modo ex deorum concilio et ex Epicuri intermundiis descendisset, Audite inquit “non futtilis commenticiasque sententias, non opificem aedificatoremque mundi Platonis de Timaeo deum, nec anum fatidicam Stoicorum Pronoeam, quam Latine licet Providentiam dicere, neque vero mundum ipsum animo et sensibus praeditum rutundum ardentem volubilem deum, portenta et miracula non disserentium philosophorum sed somniantium.
passages.english: Then Velleius, very confidently indeed, as those people usually do, fearing nothing so much as to seem to be in doubt about anything, as if he had just come down from the council of the gods and from the intermundia of Epicurus, said: "Listen to opinions that are not worthless and fabricated: not the craftsman and builder of the world, the god of Plato's Timaeus, nor the prophesying old woman of the Stoics, Pronoia, whom in Latin we may call Providence, nor yet the world itself as a god endowed with mind and senses, round, fiery, revolving — portents and marvels not of philosophers reasoning but of philosophers dreaming.
passages.notes: intermundia: the spaces between worlds where Epicurus placed the gods. Pronoia (Greek 'forethought') is given in Latin as 'Pronoeam'.

passages.original: admirabor eorum tarditatem qui animantem inmortalem et eundem beatum rutundum esse velint, quod ea forma neget ullam esse pulchriorem Plato: at mihi vel cylindri vel quadrati vel coni vel pyramidis videtur esse formosior. Quae vero vita tribuitur isti rutundo deo? nempe ut ea celeritate contorqueatur cui par nulla ne cogitari quidem possit;
passages.english: I shall marvel at the slowness of those who would have a living being that is immortal and also blessed be round, because Plato says that no shape is more beautiful than that: but to me the shape of a cylinder, or a cube, or a cone, or a pyramid seems more beautiful. And what life is assigned to that round god of yours? Why, that he should be whirled round with a speed to which nothing equal can even be imagined;
passages.notes: 'quadrati' may mean a square or cube; cube chosen for a solid figure.

passages.original: Atque etiam Xenophon paucioribus verbis eadem fere peccat; facit enim in his quae a Socrate dicta rettulit Socratem disputantem formam dei quaeri non oportere, eundemque et solem et animum deum dicere, et modo unum tum autem plures deos; quae sunt isdem in erratis fere quibus ea quae de Platone dicimus.
passages.english: And Xenophon too commits almost the same errors, in fewer words; for in the account he gave of the sayings of Socrates he represents Socrates as arguing that one ought not to ask about the form of god, and he has the same man say that both the sun and the mind are god, and at one moment that there is one god, and at another that there are several; and these involve almost the same errors as those we mention concerning Plato.

passages.original: Atque etiam Antisthenes in eo libro qui physicus inscribitur popularis deos multos naturalem unum esse dicens tollit vim et naturam deorum. Nec multo secus Speusippus Platonem avunculum subsequens et vim quandam dicens, qua omnia regantur, eamque animalem, evellere ex animis conatur cognitionem deorum.
passages.english: And Antisthenes too, in the book entitled 'The Physicist', by saying that the popular gods are many but the natural god is one, does away with the power and nature of the gods. Not very differently Speusippus, following his uncle Plato and speaking of a certain force by which all things are governed, and that an animate one, tries to root out of [our] minds the knowledge of the gods.

passages.original: atque hic idem alio loco aethera deum dicit: si intellegi potest nihil sentiens deus, qui numquam nobis occurrit neque in precibus neque in optatis neque in votis. aliis autem libris rationem quandam per omnium naturam rerum pertinentem vi divina esse adfectam putat. idem astris hoc idem tribuit, tum annis mensibus annorumque mutationibus. cum vero Hesiodi Theogoniam id est originem deorum interpretatur, tollit omnino usitatas perceptasque cognitiones deorum; neque enim Iovem neque Iunonem neque Vestam neque quemquam qui ita appelletur in deorum habet numero, sed rebus inanimis atque mutis per quandam significationem haec docet tributa nomina.
passages.english: And this same man in another place says that the ether is god: if a god that perceives nothing can be understood, one who never presents himself to us in our prayers, wishes or vows. In other books, however, he thinks that a certain reason pervading the nature of all things is endowed with divine power. He likewise attributes this same thing to the stars, then to the years, the months and the changes of the seasons. But when he interprets Hesiod's Theogony, that is, the origin of the gods, he entirely removes the customary and received notions of the gods; for he counts neither Jupiter nor Juno nor Vesta nor anyone so called among the gods, but teaches that these names were given by a kind of symbolism to inanimate and mute things.
passages.notes: 'annorumque mutationibus' probably means the changes of the seasons.

passages.original: Solus enim vidit primum esse deos, quod in omnium animis eorum notionem inpressisset ipsa natura. quae est enim gens aut quod genus hominum quod non habeat sine doctrina anticipationem quandam deorum, quam appellat pro/lhmyin Epicurus id est anteceptam animo rei quandam informationem, sine qua nec intellegi quicquam nec quaeri nec disputari potest. quoius rationis vim atque utilitatem ex illo caelesti Epicuri de regula et iudicio volumine accepimus.
passages.english: For he alone saw, first, that the gods exist, because nature herself had imprinted a notion of them in the minds of all. For what nation or what race of men is there that does not have, without teaching, a certain preconception of the gods, which Epicurus calls *prolēpsis*, that is, a certain outline of a thing grasped beforehand by the mind, without which nothing can be understood, inquired into, or argued about. The force and usefulness of this reasoning we have learned from that heavenly volume of Epicurus on the rule and criterion.
passages.notes: Greek πρόληψις transliterated in the edition as 'pro/lhmyin'.

passages.original: Quod quoniam fere constat inter omnis non philosophos solum sed etiam indoctos, fatemur constare illud etiam, hanc nos habere sive anticipationem, ut ante dixi, sive praenotionem deorum (sunt enim rebus novis nova ponenda nomina, ut Epicurus ipse pro/lhyin appellavit,
passages.english: Since this is agreed among nearly everyone, not only philosophers but also the unlearned, we acknowledge that this too is agreed, that we have either a 'preconception', as I said before, or a 'prenotion' of the gods (for new names must be given to new things, just as Epicurus himself called it *prolēpsis*,
passages.notes: Greek πρόληψιν, garbled in the scan as 'pro/lhyin'. The sentence breaks off at the end of the passage.

passages.original: Summa vero vis infinitatis et magna ac diligenti contemplatione dignissima est. in qua intellegi necesse est eam esse naturam ut omnia omnibus paribus paria respondeant; hanc i)sonomi/an appellat Epicurus id est aequabilem tributionem. ex hac igitur illud efficitur, si mortalium tanta multitudo sit, esse inmortalium non minorem, et si quae interimant innumerabilia sint, etiam ea quae conservent infinita esse debere.
passages.english: But the power of infinity is supreme, and most worthy of great and careful contemplation. In it we must understand that its nature is such that all things correspond equally to all their counterparts; this Epicurus calls *isonomia*, that is, equal distribution. From this, then, it follows that, if the multitude of mortals is so great, that of immortals is no smaller, and if the things that destroy are countless, the things that preserve must also be infinite.
passages.notes: Greek ἰσονομίαν in the edition's transliteration.

passages.original: ex quo equidem existimo tardioris ad hanc sententiam profitendam multos esse factos, quippe cum poenam ne dubitatio quidem effugere potuisset. Quid de sacrilegis, quid de impiis periurisque dicemus? Tubulus si Lucius umquam, si Lupus aut Carbo aut Neptuni filius, ut ait Lucilius, putasset esse deos, tam periurus aut tam inpurus fuisset?
passages.english: From this I for my part think that many have become slower to profess this opinion, since not even doubt had been able to escape punishment. What shall we say of the sacrilegious, of the impious and the perjured? If Lucius Tubulus, if Lupus or Carbo or the son of Neptune, as Lucilius says, had ever believed that gods exist, would he have been so perjured or so foul?
passages.notes: "Son of Neptune" is Lucilius' mocking label for some notorious figure; the person is not identified in the text.

passages.original: Hoc persaepe facitis, ut, cum aliquid non veri simile dicatis et effugere reprehensionem velitis, adferatis aliquid quod omnino ne fieri quidem possit, ut satius fuerit illud ipsum de quo ambigebatur concedere quam tam inpudenter resistere. Velut Epicurus cum videret, si atomi ferrentur in locum inferiorem suopte pondere, nihil fore in nostra potestate, quod esset earum motus certus et necessarius, invenit quo modo necessitatem effugeret, quod videlicet Democritum fugerat: ait atomum, cum pondere et gravitate directo deorsus feratur, declinare paululum.
passages.english: You very often do this: when you say something improbable and want to escape criticism, you bring forward something that could not possibly happen at all, so that it would have been better to concede the very point in dispute than to resist so shamelessly. For example, when Epicurus saw that, if atoms were carried downward by their own weight, nothing would be in our power, because their motion would be fixed and necessary, he found a way to escape necessity, which evidently had escaped Democritus: he says that the atom, while it is carried straight downward by its weight and heaviness, swerves a little.

passages.original: nihil enim olet ex Academia, nihil ne ex Lycio, nihil ne e puerilibus quidem disciplinis. Xenocraten audire potuit (quem virum, dii inmortales), et sunt qui putent audisse; ipse non vult: credo, plus nemini. Pamphilum quendam Platonis auditorem ait a se Sami auditum (ibi enim adulescens habitabat cum patre et fratribus, quod in eam pater eius Neocles agripeta venerat, sed cum agellus eum non satis aleret ut opinor, ludi magister fuit);
passages.english: For he smells of nothing from the Academy, nothing from the Lyceum, nothing even from the schoolboy disciplines. He could have heard Xenocrates (what a man, immortal gods!), and there are those who think he did hear him; he himself denies it: I believe him more than anyone. He says he heard at Samos a certain Pamphilus, a pupil of Plato (for he lived there as a young man with his father and brothers, because his father Neocles had gone there as a settler; but since, I suppose, his little plot of land did not support him well enough, he was a schoolmaster);
passages.notes: 'ne' in 'nihil ne' is probably a corruption; read as 'nihil'. Sense of 'he was a schoolmaster' refers to Neocles.

passages.original: sed hunc Platonicum mirifice contemnit Epicurus: ita metuit ne quid umquam didicisse videatur. In Nausiphane Democriteo tenetur; quem cum a se non neget auditum vexat tamen omnibus contumeliis. atqui si haec Democritea non audisset, quid audierat, quid est in physicis Epicuri non a Democrito?
passages.english: but this Platonist Epicurus wonderfully despises: so afraid is he of seeming ever to have learned anything. He is caught in the case of Nausiphanes the Democritean; though he does not deny that he heard him, he nevertheless harasses him with every insult. And yet, if he had not heard these Democritean doctrines, what had he heard? What is there in Epicurus' physics that is not from Democritus?

passages.original: cum quidem semel dicta sunt, quid est quod Velleius intellegere possit Cotta non possit? itaque corpus quid sit sanguis quid sit intellego, quasi corpus et quasi sanguis quid sit nullo prorsus modo intellego. neque tu me celas ut Pythagoras solebat alienos, nec consulto dicis occulte tamquam Heraclitus, sed, quod inter nos liceat, ne tu quidem intellegis.
passages.english: Once they have been stated, what is there that Velleius could understand and Cotta could not? So I understand what a body is and what blood is; what a quasi-body and quasi-blood are, I understand in no way at all. Nor are you hiding [it] from me as Pythagoras used to from outsiders, nor are you speaking obscurely on purpose like Heraclitus; but, if I may say so between ourselves, not even you understand [it].

passages.original: nam Phaedro nihil elegantius nihil humanius, sed stomachabatur senex si quid asperius dixeram, cum Epicurus Aristotelem vexarit contumeliosissime, Phaedoni Socratico turpissime male dixerit, Metrodori sodalis sui fratrem Timocraten, quia nescio quid in philosophia dissentiret, totis voluminibus conciderit, in Democritum ipsum quem secutus est fuerit ingratus, Nausiphanem magistrum suum, a quo non nihil didicerat, tam male acceperit. Zeno quidem non eos solum qui tum erant, Apollodorum Sillim ceteros, figebat maledictis, sed Socraten ipsum parentem philosophiae Latino verbo utens scurram Atticum fuisse dicebat, Chrysippum numquam nisi Chrysippam vocabat.
passages.english: For nothing was more refined than Phaedrus, nothing more courteous, but the old man used to get annoyed if I had said anything rather harsh; whereas Epicurus harassed Aristotle most insultingly, abused Phaedo the Socratic most disgracefully, cut to pieces in whole volumes Timocrates, the brother of his associate Metrodorus, because he disagreed on some point or other in philosophy, was ungrateful towards Democritus himself, whom he followed, and treated his teacher Nausiphanes, from whom he had learned not a little, so badly. Zeno indeed not only pierced with abuse those who were alive at the time, Apollodorus, Sillis and the rest, but said that Socrates himself, the father of philosophy, had been an Attic buffoon, using the Latin word [scurra], and never called Chrysippus anything but Chrysippa.
passages.notes: 'Sillim' (Sillis) is an uncertain name; the text may be corrupt. Zeno here is the Epicurean Zeno of Sidon.

passages.original: Ipsa vero quam nihil ad rem pertinet, quae vos delectat maxime, similitudo. quid canis nonne similis lupo (atque, ut Ennius, "simia quam similis turpissuma bestia nobis"); at mores in utroque dispares. elephanto beluarum nulla prudentior;
passages.english: But how irrelevant to the matter is that very likeness which delights you most! Is not a dog like a wolf? (and, as Ennius says, "how like us is the ape, that ugliest of beasts"); yet the habits of the two are different. No beast is wiser than the elephant;

passages.original: nam quid est quod minus probari possit, omnium in me incidere imagines, Homeri Archilochi Romuli Numae Pythagorae Platonis—nec ea forma qua illi fuerunt: quo modo illi ergo? et quorum imagines: Orpheum poetam docet Aristoteles numquam fuisse, et hoc Orphicum carmen Pythagorei ferunt cuiusdam fuisse Cerconis; at Orpheus, id est imago eius ut vos vultis, in animum meum saepe incurrit.
passages.english: For what is less capable of being proved than that the images of everyone fall upon me, of Homer, Archilochus, Romulus, Numa, Pythagoras, Plato—and not in the form in which they were: how then [are they] those men? And whose images [are they]? Aristotle teaches that the poet Orpheus never existed, and the Pythagoreans say that this Orphic poem belonged to a certain Cercon; yet Orpheus, that is, his image as you would have it, often runs into my mind.

passages.original: voluptatum credo, nempe ad corpus pertinentium; nullam enim novistis nisi profectam a corpore et redeuntem ad corpus animi voluptatem. non arbitror te velle similem esse Epicureorum reliquorum, quos pudeat quarundam Epicuri vocum, quibus ille testatur se ne intellegere quidem ullum bonum quod sit seiunctum a delicatis et obscenis voluptatibus; quas quidem non erubescens persequitur omnis nominatim.
passages.english: Of pleasures, I suppose — those pertaining to the body, of course; for you know no pleasure of the mind except one that arises from the body and returns to the body. I do not think you wish to be like the rest of the Epicureans, who are ashamed of certain sayings of Epicurus, in which he testifies that he cannot even conceive of any good that is separate from luxurious and obscene pleasures; and these, without blushing, he goes through one by one by name.

passages.original: "At etiam de sanctitate de pietate adversus deos libros scripsit Epicurus." At quo modo in his loquitur: ut Ti. Coruncanium aut P. Scaevolam pontifices maximos te audire dicas, non eum qui sustulerit omnem funditus religionem nec manibus ut Xerses sed rationibus deorum inmortalium templa et aras everterit.
passages.english: "But Epicurus also wrote books on holiness and on piety towards the gods." But how does he speak in them? So that you would say you were hearing Tiberius Coruncanius or Publius Scaevola, chief pontiffs, not the man who did away with all religion from its foundations, and overturned the temples and altars of the immortal gods not with hands, like Xerxes, but with arguments.

passages.original: Quid enim potest esse tam apertum tamque perspicuum, cum caelum suspeximus caelestiaque contemplati sumus, quam esse aliquod numen praestantissimae mentis quo haec regantur? quod ni ita esset, qui potuisset adsensu omnium dicere Ennius "aspice hoc sublime candens, quem invocant omnes Iovem"—illum vero et Iovem et dominatorem rerum et omnia motu regentem et, ut idem Ennius, "patrem divumque hominumque" et praesentem ac praepotentem deum? quod qui dubitet, haud sane intellego cur non idem sol sit an nullus sit dubitare possit;
passages.english: For what can be so plain and so evident, when we have looked up at the sky and contemplated the heavenly bodies, as that there is some divine power of surpassing intelligence by which these things are governed? If this were not so, how could Ennius have said, with the assent of all, "Look at this bright thing on high, which all invoke as Jupiter"—him indeed both as Jupiter and as lord of things, ruling all by his motion, and, as the same Ennius says, "father of gods and of men," a present and all-powerful god? Anyone who doubts this, I certainly do not understand why he could not equally doubt whether the sun exists or not;

passages.original: Cleanthes quidem noster quattuor de causis dixit in animis hominum informatas deorum esse notiones. primam posuit eam de qua modo dixi, quae orta esset ex praesensione rerum futurarum; alteram quam ceperimus ex magnitudine commodorum, quae percipiuntur caeli temperatione fecunditate terrarum aliarumque commoditatum complurium copia;
passages.english: Our Cleanthes, indeed, said that notions of the gods had been formed in human minds for four reasons. He set as the first the one I spoke of just now, which arose from foreknowledge of future events; the second, the one we have taken from the greatness of the benefits that are received from the temperate climate, the fertility of the lands, and the abundance of a great many other advantages;

passages.original: Et tamen ex ipsa hominum sollertia esse aliquam mentem et eam quidem acriorem et divinam existimare debemus. unde enim hanc homo "arripuit", ut ait apud Xenophontem Socrates. quin et umorem et calorem, qui est fusus in corpore, et terrenam ipsam viscerum soliditatem, animum denique illum spirabilem si quis quaerat unde habeamus, apparet; quorum aliud a terra sumpsimus aliud ab umore aliud ab igni aliud ab aere eo quem spiritum dicimus.
passages.english: And yet from the very ingenuity of men we ought to judge that there is some mind, and that one keener and divine. For whence did man "snatch" this, as Socrates says in Xenophon? Indeed, if anyone asks whence we have the moisture and heat diffused through the body, and the earthy solidity itself of the flesh, and finally that breathing soul, it is evident: of these we have taken one from earth, another from water, another from fire, another from that air which we call breath.

passages.original: Quod quidem Cleanthes his etiam argumentis docet, quanta vis insit caloris in omni corpore: negat enim esse ullum cibum tam gravem quin is nocte et die concoquatur; cuius etiam in reliquiis inest calor iis quas natura respuerit. iam vero venae et arteriae micare non desinunt quasi quodam igneo motu, animadversumque saepe est cum cor animantis alicuius evolsum ita mobiliter palpitaret ut imitaretur igneam celeritatem.
passages.english: Cleanthes also shows by these arguments how great a force of heat is present in every body: for he says that there is no food so heavy that it is not digested within a night and a day; and heat is present even in its remains, which nature has rejected. Moreover, the veins and arteries do not cease to throb as if with a kind of fiery motion, and it has often been observed that when the heart of some animal was torn out, it quivered so rapidly as to imitate the swiftness of fire.

passages.original: Atque ea quidem tota esse ignea duorum sensuum testimonio confirmari Cleanthes putat, tactus et oculorum. nam solis calor et candor inlustrior est quam ullius ignis, quippe qui inmenso mundo tam longe lateque conluceat, et is eius tactus est, non ut tepefaciat solum sed etiam saepe comburat, quorum neutrum faceret nisi esset igneus. "ergo" inquit "cum sol igneus sit Oceanique alatur umoribus" (quia nullus ignis sine pastu aliquo possit permanere) "necesse est aut ei similis sit igni quem adhibemus ad usum atque victum, aut ei qui corporibus animantium continetur.
passages.english: And Cleanthes thinks that it is confirmed by the testimony of two senses, touch and the eyes, that it is entirely fiery. For the heat and brightness of the sun are more brilliant than those of any fire, since it shines so far and wide over the immeasurable universe, and its touch is such that it not only warms but often also burns, neither of which it would do unless it were fiery. "Therefore," he says, "since the sun is fiery and is nourished by the moisture of Ocean" (because no fire can last without some fuel), "it must be similar either to the fire which we employ for use and living, or to that which is contained in the bodies of living creatures.

passages.original: quae si bis bina quot essent didicisset Epicurus certe non diceret; sed dum palato quid sit optimum iudicat, "caeli palatum", ut ait Ennius, non suspexit.
passages.english: Epicurus would certainly not say these things if he had learned how much two times two is; but while he judges with his palate what is best, he has not looked up at "the palate of heaven," as Ennius says.
passages.notes: Pun on palatum (palate / vault of heaven).

passages.original: nas habere—hunc igitur Ennius, ut supra dixi, nuncupat ita dicens "aspice hoc sublime candens, quem invocant omnes Iovem" planius quam alio loco idem "cui quod in me est exsecrabor hoc quod lucet quicquid est"; hunc etiam augures nostri cum dicunt "Iove fulgente tonante": dicunt enim "caelo fulgente et tonante".
passages.english: [...] to have—this, then, Ennius names, as I said above, saying "Look at this bright thing on high, which all invoke as Jupiter," more plainly than the same poet in another place: "on whom, so far as in me lies, I shall call down curses, this which shines, whatever it is"; this too our augurs [mean] when they say "when Jupiter flashes and thunders": for they mean "when the sky flashes and thunders."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-word ("nas habere"); the preceding text is missing.

passages.original: et formae enim nobis deorum et aetates et vestitus ornatusque noti sunt, genera praeterea coniugia cognationes, omniaque traducta ad similitudinem inbecillitatis humanae. nam et perturbatis animis inducuntur: accepimus enim deorum cupiditates aegritudines iracundias; nec vero, ut fabulae ferunt, bellis proeliisque caruerunt, nec solum ut apud Homerum cum duo exercitus contrarios alii dei ex alia parte defenderent, sed etiam ut cum Titanis ut cum Gigantibus sua propria bella gesserunt. haec et dicuntur et creduntur stultissime et plena sunt futtilitatis summaeque levitatis.
passages.english: For the forms of the gods, their ages, clothing and adornment are known to us, and besides their families, marriages and kinships, and everything has been brought into the likeness of human weakness. For they are also represented with disturbed minds: we have heard of the desires, griefs and fits of anger of the gods; nor indeed, as the stories relate, were they without wars and battles, and not only as in Homer, when two armies were opposed and different gods defended them from either side, but they also waged their own wars, as with the Titans, as with the Giants. These things are both said and believed most foolishly, and are full of nonsense and the utmost frivolity.

passages.original: Sunt autem qui omnia naturae nomine appellent, ut Epicurus qui ita dividit, omnium quae sint naturam esse corpora et inane quaeque is accidant. Sed nos cum dicimus natura constare administrarique mundum, non ita dicimus ut glaebam aut fragmentum lapidis aut aliquid eius modi nulla cohaerendi natura, sed ut arborem ut animal, in quibus nulla temeritas sed ordo apparet et artis quaedam similitudo.
passages.english: There are some, however, who call everything by the name of nature, like Epicurus, who divides [things] thus: the nature of all things that exist is bodies and void and what happens to them. But when we say that the world is composed and governed by nature, we do not mean it as [one would of] a clod or a fragment of stone or something of that kind with no natural principle of coherence, but as [of] a tree or an animal, in which no randomness but order appears, and a certain likeness to art.

passages.original: utque ille apud Accium pastor, qui navem numquam ante vidisset, ut procul divinum et novum vehiculum Argonautarum e monte conspexit, primo admirans et perterritus hoc modo loquitur: tanta moles labitur fremibunda ex alto ingenti sonitu et spiritu: prae se undas volvit, vertices vi suscitat, ruit prolapsa, pelagus respergit reflat;ita dum interruptum credas nimbum volvier,dum quod sublime ventis expulsum rapi saxum aut procellis, vel globosos turbines existere ictos undis concursantibus—nisi quas terrestres pontus strages conciet aut forte Triton fuscina evertens specus subter radices penitus undanti in freto molem ex profundo saxeam ad caelum eruit: dubitat primo quae sit ea natura quam cernit ignotam;
passages.english: And as that shepherd in Accius, who had never before seen a ship, when from a mountain he caught sight far off of the divine and novel vessel of the Argonauts, at first wondering and terrified, speaks in this way: "So vast a mass glides roaring from the deep with mighty sound and blast: it rolls the waves before it, stirs up whirlpools by its force, rushes headlong, sprinkles back and blows back the sea; so that now you might believe a broken storm-cloud was rolling, now that some rock flung up on high was swept along by winds or storms, or that round whirlwinds were rising, struck by the clashing waves—unless it is some destruction of the land that the sea stirs up, or perhaps Triton, overturning caverns with his trident beneath the roots deep in the surging strait, is heaving up a rocky mass from the depths to the sky": he at first doubts what this unknown nature is that he sees;
passages.notes: The verse is difficult and its syntax loose; rendered as plausibly as the text allows.

passages.original: tritum est enim pro Latino. hunc rursus amplectitur inmensus aether, qui constat ex altissimis ignibus (mutuemur hoc quoque verbum, dicaturque tam aether Latine quam dicitur aer, etsi interpretatur Pacuvius: "hoc, quod memoro, nostri caelum Grai perhibent aethera"—quasi vero non Graius hoc dicat. "at Latine loquitur." si quidem nos non quasi Graece loquentem audiamus; docet idem alio loco:
passages.english: for it has become common as if Latin. This [air] in turn is embraced by the boundless aether, which consists of the highest fires (let us borrow this word too, and let aether be said in Latin just as aer is said, although Pacuvius translates it: "this, which I speak of, our people call the sky, the Greeks aether"—as though it were not a Greek who says this. "But he speaks in Latin." Yes, if we do not hear him as if speaking Greek; the same poet teaches in another place:

passages.original: Praeclare ergo Aristoteles "Si essent" inquit "qui sub terra semper habitavissent bonis et inlustribus domiciliis, quae essent ornata signis atque picturis instructaque rebus his omnibus quibus abundant i qui beati putantur, nec tamen exissent umquam supra terram, accepissent autem fama et auditione esse quoddam numen et vim deorum, deinde aliquo tempore patefactis terrae faucibus ex illis abditis sedibus evadere in haec loca quae nos incolimus atque exire potuissent: cum repente terram et maria caelumque vidissent, nubium magnitudinem ventorumque vim cognovissent aspexissentque solem eiusque cum magnitudinem pulchritudinemque tum etiam efficientiam cognovissent, quod is diem efficeret toto caelo luce diffusa, cum autem terras nox opacasset tum caelum totum cernerent astris distinctum et ornatum lunaeque luminum varietatem tum crescentis tum senescentis, eorumque omnium ortus et occasus atque in omni aeternitate ratos inmutabilesque cursus—quae cum viderent, profecto et esse deos et haec tanta opera
passages.english: Splendidly, then, Aristotle says: "If there were people who had always lived beneath the earth in good and bright dwellings, adorned with statues and paintings and furnished with all the things in which those thought happy abound, and yet had never come out above the earth, but had learned by report and hearsay that there exists a certain divine power and force of gods; and then at some time, the jaws of the earth being opened, they had been able to escape from those hidden abodes and come out into these regions which we inhabit: when they suddenly saw the earth and the seas and the sky, came to know the size of the clouds and the force of the winds, and beheld the sun and came to know not only its size and beauty but also its power, in that it makes the day by spreading light over the whole sky; and when night had darkened the lands, they then saw the whole sky studded and adorned with stars, and the varied light of the moon, now waxing, now waning, and the risings and settings of all these, and their courses fixed and unchangeable through all eternity—when they saw these things, they would surely [believe] both that gods exist and that these great works

passages.original: sus vero quid habet praeter escam; cui quidem ne putesceret animam ipsam pro sale datam dicit esse Chrysippus; qua pecude, quod erat ad vescendum hominibus apta, nihil genuit natura fecundius. quid multitudinem suavitatemque piscium dicam, quid avium; ex quibus tanta percipitur voluptas, ut interdum Pronoea nostra Epicurea fuisse videatur, atque eae ne caperentur quidem nisi hominum ratione atque sollertia;
passages.english: As for the pig, what does it have except food? Chrysippus indeed says that its very soul was given to it in place of salt, so that it would not go rotten; and because this animal was fit for humans to eat, nature produced nothing more prolific. What should I say of the abundance and pleasantness of fish, or of birds? From these such great pleasure is gained that at times our Providence seems to have been an Epicurean; and they would not even be caught except by human reason and skill;
passages.notes: 'putesceret' read as 'putesceret/putresceret' (rot). 'Pronoea' is Greek for Providence.

passages.original: At enim quaerit apud Xenophontem Socrates unde animum arripuerimus si nullus fuerit in mundo. Et ego quaero unde orationem unde numeros unde cantus; nisi vero loqui solem cum luna putamus cum propius accesserit, aut ad harmoniam canere mundum ut Pythagoras existimat. Naturae ista sunt Balbe, naturae non artificiose ambulantis ut ait Zeno, quod quidem quale sit iam videbimus, sed omnia cientis et agitantis motibus et mutationibus suis.
passages.english: But, [you say], Socrates in Xenophon asks where we got our mind from, if there was none in the world. And I ask where [we got] speech from, where numbers, where songs; unless indeed we think that the sun talks with the moon when it has come nearer, or that the world sings in harmony, as Pythagoras supposes. These things belong to nature, Balbus, to a nature not 'proceeding artistically', as Zeno says (and what that means we shall see presently), but setting all things in motion and stirring them by its own movements and changes.
passages.notes: 'Artificiose ambulantis' renders Zeno's Stoic definition of nature as a craftsmanlike fire proceeding methodically; 'proceeding artistically' is an approximation.

passages.original: Nam quos ab hominibus pervenisse dicis ad deos, tu reddes rationem quem ad modum id fieri potuerit aut cur fieri desierit, et ego discam libenter; quo modo nunc quidem est, non video quo pacto ille, cui "in monte Oetaeo inlatae lampades" fuerint ut ait Accius, "in domum aeternam patris" ex illo ardore pervenerit; quem tamen Homerus apud inferos conveniri facit ab Ulixe sicut ceteros qui excesserant vita.
passages.english: For as to those who you say have passed from men to gods, you will give an account of how that could have happened or why it has ceased to happen, and I will gladly learn; as things now stand, I do not see how he for whom "torches were brought on Mount Oeta," as Accius says, passed from that blaze "into the eternal home of his father"; yet Homer makes him be met by Ulysses among the dead, like the others who had departed life.
passages.notes: The one meant is Heracles (Hercules), burned on Mount Oeta.

passages.original: quamquam Circen quoque coloni nostri Cercienses religiose colunt. ergo hanc deam ducis: quid Medeae respondebis, quae duobus dis avis Sole et Oceano Aeeta patre matre Idyia procreata est, quid huius Absyrtio fratri (qui est apud Pacuvium Aegialeus, sed illud nomen veterum litteris usitatius)? qui si di non sunt, vereor quid agat Ino; haec enim omnia ex eodem fonte fluxerunt.
passages.english: And yet Circe too is devoutly worshipped by our colonists at Circeii. So you count her a goddess: what answer will you give Medea, who was born of two gods as grandfathers, the Sun and Ocean, with Aeetes as father and Idyia as mother? What [answer will you give] her brother Absyrtus (who in Pacuvius is Aegialeus, but the former name is more common in the writings of the ancients)? If these are not gods, I fear for what will become of Ino; for all these [claims] have flowed from the same source.
passages.notes: "Circen" is the Greek accusative of Circe, and "Cercienses" is evidently the people of Circeii. "Absyrtio" is taken as dative of Absyrtus, governed by an understood "respondebis".
